E0587.summary: Basil Valentine's term for what nature holds concealed, to be sought with one's own eyes and hand as the basis for judging rightly.
E0587.body: Spoken by Basil Valentine (“the monk”), as quoted by Atwood: “Learn and look for the first foundation, says the monk, which nature holds concealed” [III.1 ¶13]. The record presents it as something to be sought personally, with one's own eyes and hand, and as the basis for philosophizing with judgment.

E0588.summary: In the Platonic Successor's account, the highest principle, beyond all and more ineffable than all, celebrated first as unfolding the Intelligible Universe.
E0588.body: A view quoted from the Platonic Successor [II.4 ¶41]. The First God is celebrated first as unfolding the Intelligible Universe and only last as producing earth, heavens and souls. He is praised “as the God of all gods, the Unity of all unities, and beyond the First Adyta” and “as more ineffable than all silence, and more Unknown than all recondite essence” [II.4 ¶41].

E0589.summary: Atwood's term for the original life about whose penetralia consciousness is drawn in Hades, and from whose perpetual motion the nether darkness flows.
E0589.body: In Atwood's own voice: consciousness in Hades is drawn about the penetralia of the first life, and the nether darkness is described as “flowing out from the perpetual motion of the first life” [II.3 ¶18].

E0590.summary: In Plotinus as quoted, the light shining primarily in itself, at once illuminating and illuminated, and the foundation of every intellect.
E0590.body: Quoted from Plotinus [III.2 ¶66]. The First Light shines primarily in itself and “at one and the same time illuminates and is illuminated” [III.2 ¶66]. It is identified with the ground of intellect: “this First Light, which is the foundation of every intellect and primarily knows itself” [III.2 ¶66].

E0591.summary: Albertus Magnus's definition: an unctuous subtle humidity forcibly incorporated with a subtle earthy part.
E0591.body: Quoted from Albertus Magnus: “the first material of the metals is an unctuous subtle humidity, forcibly incorporated with a subtle terrestreity” [I.2 ¶29].

E0592.summary: The one subject of the Art: the common root substance of all natures, not found on earth or among sensible things, reached by going back in consciousness to the original of life.
E0592.body:
**Atwood's account.** The First Matter is the common basis to which bodies can be reduced and from which they take new form — “their common basis or mercurial first matter” [I.2 ¶3] — and so the true subject of transmutation; she equates it with the “Universal Subject” [I.2 ¶7] and the “Universal Matter of the adepts”, which ordinary analysis does not discover [I.2 ¶3]. It is not any sensible thing but a middle substance generated from the Universal Spirit's active and passive relations, “the simple generated substance of life and light, immanifestly flowing throughout nature” [I.2 ¶34]; “the First Matter is indeed the union of masculine and feminine spirits” [I.2 ¶33]; “Thus obscure, after all, is the true Matter of the Alchemists” [I.2 ¶34]. Albert describes it “with the characteristic minuteness of personal observation” [I.1 ¶39]; Vaughan's Lumen de Lumine gives “an allegorical display of the first matter” [I.1 ¶74]. The alchemists claim for it extreme attributes and miraculous origin, as the Greeks do for the ethereal hypostasis [III.1 ¶3].

**Identities.** It is generated by an emancipation of the Fontal Source, “and this is Diana, and that refulgent Light which eclipses every other light but that of its proper Reason” [III.1 ¶70]. It is “the abyssal Darkness”, brought forth by God as First Matter [III.2 ¶56]; it is not known in energy “but flies from him, indeed, who wishes intently to behold” [III.2 ¶57]. Beyond all things it is “That which is prior to all things” [III.2 ¶66]. Footnoted identities: “very natural true sperm of the greater world”, and Sendivogius's “water of our sea, the water of life, not wetting the hands” [III.2 n43]. Chapter III.3 treats its manifestation and “Information by Light” [III.3 ¶1].

**Quoted voices.** Mylius: God “creavit unam substantiam; hanc primam materiam nominamus” (ours: created one substance; this we name the first matter) [III.2 ¶2; also III.2 ¶56]. Basil Valentine: the all-containing water formed into earth by the dryness of its fire and air is “the first matter of all things” [III.2 ¶19]. Vaughan: “The eye of man never saw her twice under one and the same shape” [II.3 ¶30], calling it the mineral nature; knowing it is discovering “the Sanctuary of Nature” [III.4 ¶44]. The Rosy Cross: “O, most excellent subject! Out of which all things in the world are generated” — poison named “the flying eagle”, and “the Seed of Divine benediction”, hidden from the wicked by its vestures, parent of the philosophical Sun and Moon [III.3 ¶63]. Arnold: the Stone is dissolved “that it may be reduced into its first Matter” [IV.1 ¶7]; Khunrath: the Azoth “reduces bodies to their First Matter” [IV.3 ¶28] and it appears as wet, impure “mud earth” partaking of Adam [IV.1 ¶36]. Eudoxus: Mercury, “Our Old Man”, “is the first matter of all metals” [IV.3 ¶10]. Flamel: “I had now the prima material, the first principles, yet not their preparation” [I.1 ¶57].

**Appendix (Table Talk, later layer).** It is not found on earth but reached by going back in consciousness to the original of life. “It is immediately antecedent to the first consciousness” and presents itself “as the extreme of bound and definiteness reverting to non- being” [APP ¶137]; its attributes are transmutable forms, hence seeming contradictions. Elsewhere, “the First Mater which is humanly producible” may be unlawfully formed for a finite end [APP ¶37].

E0593.summary: In Paracelsus as quoted, the invisible, intangible life present in all things — the life the creatures have.
E0593.body: Quoted from Paracelsus: “This is the First Matter of the elements, which can neither be seen nor felt, and yet is in all things” [I.2 ¶26]; it is “nothing else but that life which the creatures have” [I.2 ¶26].

E0594.summary: In Atwood's words, the One with whom one would move and whose Will one would be, at once the Antecedent and Final Cause of all.
E0594.body: Atwood asks who can “move One with the First Mover, and Be His Will, who is at once the Antecedent and Final Cause of all” [III.3 ¶78].

E0595.summary: In Eirenaeus as quoted, the laborious manual first stage of the work, disposing the matter as first found, contrasted with the Second where Nature works alone.
E0595.body: Eirenaeus's term, as quoted: “there is no work more tedious than our First Operation” [IV.1 ¶6], and “nothing can be achieved in the First Operation without sweating and much labor” [IV.1 ¶11]. It concerns disposing the matter as first found and is contrasted with the Second Operation, in which Nature works alone.

E0596.summary: In Vaughan as quoted, the first part of the Gross Work, which Agrippa knew and made clear; not described further.
E0596.body: Vaughan says Agrippa “knew the First Preparation, and has clearly discovered it” [IV.1 ¶36]. The packet gives no description of the preparation itself.

E0597.summary: Atwood's term for the subject in its first prepared state, which she says is meant by the Lunar Vulcan and is also called Diana.
E0597.body: In Atwood's voice: by “the Lunar Vulcan, as we long ago suggested, is meant the first prepared Subject”, “which is also called Diana, and the secret natural interior Fire of Adepts” [IV.1 ¶29].

E0598.summary: What the theurgically prepared seeker rises to: the most united in nature, its Flower, through which it is Deity.
E0598.body: Atwood, following “the doctrine of the ancients”: “if any one wish to discover the First Principle, according to the doctrine of the ancients, he must be theurgically prepared” [III.3 ¶59]. It is described as the most united in nature, its Flower, that through which it is Deity, suspended from its fountain and holding the Universe in sympathetic consent with itself [III.3 ¶59].

E0599.summary: Lully's name for the chaotic, monster-shaped spirits, which Atwood explains by the Seed of Spirit found in their purified material extreme.
E0599.body: Atwood reports: “But Lully, indeed, calls these chaotic forms first principles” [II.3 ¶30], and calls the first principles of the Art “Spiritus fugitives in aero condensators” (fugitive spirits condensed in the air) [II.3 ¶30]. Atwood explains the name: they are so called because the Seed of Spirit is found in their purified material extreme, not because they are permanent or rational [II.3 ¶30].

E0600.summary: Atwood's phrase for the stage of life in which the true Light, as distinct from common light, becomes efficient.
E0600.body: Atwood speaks of the true Light, distinct from common light, as “that which in the first rotary wheel of life becomes efficient” [IV.3 ¶30]. Not further explained.

E0601.summary: Atwood's term for the origin from which every advance in externals leads man further away.
E0601.body: Atwood: “every advance we make in externals leads us further off from the First Source” [IV.4 ¶18].

E0602.summary: In Atwood's words, what man may know really and experimentally — the highest privilege he can propose.
E0602.body: Atwood presents as man's highest privilege “to know the First Truth of things really and experimentally” [IV.4 ¶22].

E0603.summary: What the sought insoluble, transmuting, uniting union requires; voice unclear.
E0603.body: Voice unclear in the record: “such a tie cannot be without the first unity” [III.1 ¶50]. The context links creating and transmuting without violence to the first power, wisdom and love.

E0604.summary: In the Appendix, the green first stage of life, identified with hope as the first aspiration to progress, whose ripened Life is purple.
E0604.body: From the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), in Atwood's voice: “The first vegetative life is green, it arises with hope; it is hope” [APP ¶119]; “The purple color is its ripened Life” [APP ¶119].

E0605.summary: In Eirenaeus as quoted, the work accomplished by assiduity and industry, with the Divine blessing and a good principle to begin with.
E0605.body: Eirenaeus: “it is by assiduity and industry that we accomplish the First Work” [IV.1 ¶6], with the Divine blessing and a good principle to begin with.

E0606.summary: In the Appendix, the early results of the work: real but not permanent, to be sacrificed for the promise they contain.
E0606.body: From the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood: “The first-fruits, tough perfectly real, should not be accepted as permanent” [APP ¶74]; they are to be sacrificed for the promise they contain.

E0607.summary: In Atwood's account, the third operation: after calcinations, a reunion into a more permanent form of Being.
E0607.body: Atwood describes fixation as the operation in which “after calcinations there is a reunion into a more permanent form of Being” [III.2 ¶64].

E0608.summary: The two contrary states the work inverts and unites: the fixed made volatile and the volatile fixed, until both reach perfect Fixity.
E0608.body: Atwood describes the work as “that which is fixed becoming volatile and the volatile nature fixed” [I.2 ¶20]. In Part IV (voice unclear) “the fixed is made volatile” in the dissolution, wholly so in the Second Operation [IV.1 ¶36], and the fixed must be separated “from the unfixed” [IV.1 ¶40]; fixed Antimony reaches fixed disease [IV.1]. Eudoxus, quoted, makes the compound of Art from the union of the two, which act on each other until they “are volatilized and fixed reciprocally into a perfect Fixity” [IV.3 ¶9].

E0609.summary: In the Democritus passage, material drawn out and worked on the coals until it appears Golden.
E0609.body: Quoted from Democritus: “Drawing the fixed Brass out bodily” [IV.1 ¶43], it is worked on the coals until it appears Golden.

E0610.summary: In the Author of the Open Entrance, silver (for the white) or gold (for the red), melted with the Stone in projection.
E0610.body: The Author of the Open Entrance directs “four parts of one of the fixed metals, i.e., silver of it be for the white, or gold if it be for the red” [IV.3 ¶20] to be used with the Stone in projection.

E0611.summary: In Eudoxus as quoted, the salt extracted from the earth by washing it with its spirit, in which Mercury's whole energy consists; the Blood of our Stone.
E0611.body: Eudoxus calls it “the Fixed Salt, which is the Blood of our Stone” [IV.3 ¶7]. It is extracted from the earth by washing it with its spirit, and the whole energy of Mercury consists in it; distilled water “carries up with it a part of this fiery salt” [IV.3 ¶9].

E0612.summary: The balsam of nature that preserves bodies (per the Scholiast), and the Philosophers' Stone into which fixed Mercury turns (per The Triumph).
E0612.body: Atwood reports the Scholiast's view: “The fixed sulfur of adepts, according to our Scholiast, is the true balsam of nature” [I.3 n61]; “The more anything abounds with this balsam, the longer it lives and is preserved from perishing” [I.3 n61], and the universal medicine is concreted from things rich in it. The author of The Triumph makes the fixed and nourished Mercury become “the fixed Sulphur, which is the Stone of Philosophers” [IV.2 ¶6].

E0613.summary: Something fixed which must be rendered volatile and returned free; knowing how admits one to the temple of Divine Science.
E0613.body: Atwood speaks of knowing “how to render the fixed tincture of life volatile, and to return it, being free” [IV.4 ¶32] as admission to the temple of Divine Science. Not further explained.

E0614.summary: In Bloomfield as quoted, the three ‘persons’ to be joined in one until they taste death and live together.
E0614.body: Quoted from Bloomfield: “The Fixt, the Variable, and the Fugitive” [IV.2 ¶36] are three persons to be joined in one until they taste death and live together.

E0615.summary: An adept whose own account of finding, preparing and projecting the Stone Atwood quotes at length, and whom she cites repeatedly as an authority on the matter and fire.
E0615.body:
Atwood quotes Nicholas Flamel's own account at length as a remarkable, well-known case: the book, its explanation, the preparation, projection and the moral effect of the Stone — “I had now the prima material, the first principles, yet not their preparation” [I.1 ¶56, I.1 ¶57]. Sources named are his Hieroglyphics and Testament; listed writings include La Sommaire Philosophique (in French verse, translated in the Theatrum Chemicum), Le Desir desiree and Le Grand Eclaircissement [I.1 ¶58]. His Summario Philosophico gave extracts from Democritus [I.1 ¶12, I.1 n16]. He is named with Rupicessa, De Meun, Pontanus, Basil Valentine and Ripley among genuine seekers, contrasted with the spurious brood of idlers [I.1 ¶49].

Atwood uses him as an example: though he had matter, fire and furnace from Abraham the Jew, he still wandered three years [III.1 ¶37]. His Summula supports the alchemists' garden, “where the sun as well morning as evening remains with a most sweet dew” [II.4 ¶9, II.4 n4], and the nature of the fire — not coal or wood but “a bright shining fire like the Sun itself, whose heat must neither be excessive, but always of one and the same degree” [IV.1 ¶41, IV.1 n35]. His Second Book is cited for learned discretion [IV.1 ¶29]. He is cited alongside Artefius [IV.3 ¶7] and speaks “more particularly” on the two Mercuries: “one must make use of the citrine Mercury to make the Imbibition of the Red”, warning he was himself deceived until the Jew informed him [IV.3 ¶10]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) he is compared for the macrocosm's image evolved before the mental eye in regeneration [APP ¶55].

E0616.summary: An Arabian name for the Matter which Atwood says truly designates the substant hypothesis, identified with Magnesia and the water that wets not the hands.
E0616.body: In Atwood's voice, by this Arabian name “thus the substant hypothesis is said very truly to be designated” [III.2 ¶8]. She equates it with several names: “the white sand, Quellum, which Van Helmont speaks of”; “this salt is the Water that wets not the hands”; “that identical Magnesia that was exhibited in the Mysteries”; and “the White Island of Vishnu; the Lord of Radha; the White Paradise” [III.2 ¶8].
